item.text:
**Bottom Line**
No. The strongest 2024 evidence points away from genuine acceptance that power should be contestable through free, fair, and meaningful elections. There is limited pro evidence that the election was processed through formal institutions and that opposition parties still won seats, but those signals are weak and sit alongside widespread fraud allegations, opposition distrust of the courts, disputed inauguration, and later term-limit revision plans.

- [Congo’s election commission cancels 82 candidates in disputed December polling](https://theprint.in/world/congos-election-commission-cancels-82-candidates-in-disputed-december-polling/1913556/) | Reuters | 2024-01-07 | CENI canceled votes for 82 legislative candidates over alleged fraud and other issues. The government and election commission still publicly defended the poll as free and fair, which is the best limited pro evidence for acceptance of electoral contestation, but the same report shows major procedural breakdowns and renewed calls for a rerun. | `4B.1`
- [President Tshisekedi’s ruling party leads in Congo legislative election](https://theprint.in/world/president-tshisekedis-ruling-party-leads-in-congo-legislative-election/1923188/) | Reuters | 2024-01-14 | UDPS and allied parties won seats from an election that still produced multiple parties in parliament, so the system remained electorally competitive in a formal sense. But the report also notes fraud allegations and transparency concerns, so this is only weak counterevidence. | `4B.1`
- [DR Congo constitutional court rejects petitions against provisional election results](https://theprint.in/world/dr-congo-constitutional-court-rejects-petitions-against-provisional-election-results/1917177/) | Reuters | 2024-01-10 | The court rejected challenges and confirmed Tshisekedi’s victory, but the main opponents refused to use the court because they did not trust state institutions. That is strong evidence against meaningful acceptance of contestable power through trusted elections. | `4B.1`
- [Congolese President Tshisekedi sworn in for second term after disputed vote](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/congolese-president-tshisekedi-sworn-in-for-second-term-after-disputed-vote-3278886) | Reuters | 2024-01-20 | Tshisekedi was inaugurated after a landslide victory that opponents refused to recognize because of widespread irregularities. This is direct negative evidence that he did not enter office on a broadly accepted free-and-fair mandate. | `4B.1`
- [Congo President Tshisekedi draws criticism over constitutional reform plans](https://theprint.in/world/congo-president-tshisekedi-draws-criticism-over-constitutional-reform-plans/2327398/) | Reuters | 2024-10-24 | Tshisekedi announced a commission to consider revising the constitution in ways that could remove term limits and enable a third term. That is strong evidence against genuine acceptance of open-ended electoral contestability. | `4B.1`
- [Democratic Republic of Congo: Freedom in the World 2024 Country Report](https://freedomhouse.org/country/democratic-republic-congo/freedom-world/2024) | Freedom House | 2024 | Freedom House describes Congo’s political system as manipulated by elites, with severe electoral problems, intimidation of opposition, and a broader pattern of constrained competition. This is contextual but strong negative evidence for 4B.1. | `4B.1`

**Search Gap**
I did not find convincing positive evidence that Tshisekedi personally embraced the principle that he could lose power in a genuinely free, fair, and meaningful election. The available pro evidence is mostly procedural or self-serving: formal court validation, official claims that the poll was fair, and the fact that opposition parties still won some legislative seats. The weight of the record points the other way, especially once the October 2024 term-limit reform push is included.
